title: GMROI: formula, worked example, and how buyers use it
summary: GMROI is gross margin divided by average inventory at cost. See the formula, a worked example by category, and why a 30% margin category can return 3.43.
body_markdown:
**By Elie Dufeu, CTO & Co-Founder, Metreecs.** Published 20 November 2026.


GMROI (gross margin return on inventory) is gross margin divided by average inventory at cost. It tells you how much gross margin each euro held in stock earned over a period, so a GMROI of 2.40 means €2.40 of margin for every €1 of average inventory.


Buyers tend to rank categories by margin rate, and finance tends to rank them by turnover. The two rankings often disagree, because a high margin and a fast turn rarely come together. In the worked example below, the category with the thinnest margin (30%) earns the highest return on its stock, and a category that keeps 45% of every sale earns the lowest.


This guide walks through the GMROI formula on one retailer, the averaging choice that moves the same category from 2.40 to 3.20, what public data says about a "good" number, and how buyers read the ratio category by category. If you would rather run that reading on your own range, you can[review your category returns with our team](https://www.metreecs.com/form/discover) .


**Key Takeaways**


- GMROI = gross margin ÷ average inventory at cost. A category with €480k of gross margin and €200k of average inventory has a GMROI of 2.40.
- US clothing stores earned a gross margin of 49.6% of sales in 2022, against 28.7% for food and beverage stores (US Census Bureau, Annual Retail Trade Survey). In September 2026, clothing stores held 2.01 months of sales in stock and food and beverage stores 0.82.
- In a 2005 Management Science study of 311 listed retailers over 1987 to 2000, a model built on gross margin, capital intensity, and sales surprise explained 97.2% of the total variation in inventory turnover (Gaur, Fisher, and Raman).
- The averaging method changes the answer: the same seasonal category shows 3.20 with a two-point average and 2.40 with 13 month-end stock values.
- In our worked example, a category with a 30% margin returns 3.43 and a category with a 45% margin returns 1.23.


## What is GMROI?


GMROI, or gross margin return on inventory investment, measures the gross margin a retailer earns for each unit of currency invested in stock. It is calculated as gross margin divided by average inventory at cost over the same period, usually 12 months. A result of 2.0 means every €1 of average inventory produced €2 of gross margin.


You will also see it written GMROII, with the second I standing for investment, and the calculation is identical. It is a merchandising metric more than an accounting one. Finance teams already track[working capital tied up in inventory](https://www.metreecs.com/blog/working-capital-inventory) at company level, and GMROI asks the same question of a category, a brand, or a single product.


Its value is that it joins two numbers retailers usually read apart. Margin rate says how much you keep from each sale, and turnover says how quickly stock converts into sales. Because the ratio multiplies the two effects, it can rank a modest-margin line that sells every week above a prestige line that sits for months.


Research on listed retailers shows the same trade-off. In a Wharton working paper covering 1978 to 1997, Vishal Gaur, Marshall Fisher, and Ananth Raman found that retail segments reach similar returns on assets with very different mixes of gross margin and inventory turns, and that within a segment high gross margin goes with low turns. Their later study in Management Science (2005) covered 311 listed retailers over 1987 to 2000, and its model built on gross margin, capital intensity, and sales surprise explained 97.2% of the total variation in inventory turnover.


## The GMROI formula, with a worked example


**GMROI = gross margin ÷ average inventory at cost**


Gross margin is net sales minus cost of goods sold (COGS), in currency and after markdowns. Average inventory at cost is the average value of the stock you held over the period, valued at what you paid for it. Both figures must cover the same products and the same period.


Take an outdoor equipment retailer and its footwear category (an illustrative example with our own arithmetic, reused in every section).


1. Net sales over 12 months: €1,200k.
2. COGS: €720k, so gross margin is €1,200k minus €720k = €480k, or 40% of sales.
3. Average inventory at cost, from 13 month-end stock values: €200k.
4. GMROI: €480k ÷ €200k = 2.40.


Each euro kept in footwear stock brought back €2.40 of gross margin over the year. Some retailers write the same result as 240% or as €2.40, and the meaning does not change.


### GMROI, margin rate, and turnover


The formula splits into two familiar ratios:


**GMROI = gross margin % x (net sales ÷ average inventory at cost)**


For footwear, that is 40% x (€1,200k ÷ €200k), or 0.40 x 6.0 = 2.40. The second term is sometimes called the sales-to-stock ratio. It resembles inventory turnover, but turnover divides COGS by average inventory, which gives 3.6 turns here.


You can also start from turnover: GMROI = turnover x (gross margin ÷ COGS). With 3.6 turns and €480k of margin on €720k of COGS, the result is 3.6 x 0.667 = 2.40. A team already working on[improving inventory turnover](https://www.metreecs.com/blog/inventory-turnover-improvement) is therefore moving one of the two drivers, and the margin rate is the other.


### Which average inventory to use


Most disagreements about a GMROI figure come from the denominator. The quick method averages opening and closing stock for the year. The more reliable method averages 13 month-end values (the opening figure plus 12 month-ends), which captures the build-up before a season.


Here is an illustrative case. Daniel is the financial controller of the outdoor retailer. Footwear stock stood at €150k at the start of the year and at €150k again at the end, so his first calculation gave €480k ÷ €150k = 3.20.


The buying team did not recognise the number, because footwear stock peaks at €290k ahead of the hiking season. With the 13 month-end values, average inventory came to €200k and the result to 2.40. Both figures describe the same year of trading, sampled in two different ways.


One mistake we repeatedly see is a ratio built from mismatched valuations, with gross margin taken from the sales ledger and inventory taken at retail value from the merchandising system. Stock at retail value inflates the denominator and understates the return. Value the stock at cost, with the same costing method (weighted average or FIFO) that produced the COGS.


## What is a good GMROI?


There is no universal threshold, and the "2 to 3" rule of thumb repeated in many guides rarely comes with a source. A GMROI above 1.0 only says that a year of gross margin exceeds the average value of the stock. That margin still has to pay for stores, staff, logistics, and the[cost of carrying inventory](https://www.metreecs.com/blog/inventory-carrying-cost) , so a category at 1.1 is probably losing money once those costs are counted.


Public statistics explain why targets differ so much from one sector to the next. The US Census Bureau's Annual Retail Trade Survey reports gross margin as a percentage of sales by kind of business, and its monthly retail series report how many months of sales each sector holds in stock.


Kind of business (US)Gross margin, % of sales (2022)Inventories to sales ratio, months (September 2026)Implied return on inventory (our arithmetic)Clothing and clothing accessories stores49.6%2.01about 3.0Food and beverage stores28.7%0.82about 4.2All retail31.1%1.35about 2.8


The last column is our own rough calculation: margin rate x 12 ÷ the ratio. It mixes two different years and compares month-end stock with one month of sales, so read it as an order of magnitude and never as a published benchmark. Food and beverage stores keep a much lower margin rate than clothing stores and still earn more per euro of stock, because they hold about 40% of the cover.


Internal comparisons are more useful than any sector average. Compare each category with its own GMROI a year earlier, with the other categories competing for the same budget, and with the return the business needs to cover its costs. Across Metreecs' work with multi-category retailers, the ranking of categories by return on inventory rarely matches the margin ranking the buying team carries in its head.


## How buyers use GMROI by category


A company-level GMROI hides more than it shows. Here are the outdoor retailer's four categories over the same 12 months (illustrative figures).


CategoryNet salesGross margin %Gross marginAverage inventory at costTurnoverGMROIFootwear€1,200k40%€480k€200k3.62.40Technical apparel€1,800k55%€990k€450k1.82.20Tents and sleeping bags€900k45%€405k€330k1.51.23Camping accessories€800k30%€240k€70k8.03.43Total€4,700k45%€2,115k€1,050k2.52.01


Technical apparel has the best margin rate and the largest margin in euros, yet it returns less than footwear because it needs €450k of stock to run. Tents keep 45% of each sale and return only 1.23. Camping accessories, the category with the thinnest margin, return 3.43.


Léa, the retailer's head of buying, had planned to shrink the accessories range and give the budget to apparel (another illustrative case). Her argument was the margin rate, 30% against 55%. The table showed her that each euro moved from accessories stock to apparel stock would earn €2.20 where it had been earning €3.43, so she kept the range and turned her attention to tents.


### Allocating the buying budget


The ratio is most useful when the next euro of stock has to go somewhere. In[open-to-buy planning](https://www.metreecs.com/blog/open-to-buy-planning) , a category with a high and stable return is a candidate for more budget, provided the extra stock would sell at the same margin. A category with a low return needs a diagnosis before it gets a cut.


That condition matters. GMROI is an average over the stock already held, and the next euro seldom earns the average. More depth on accessories that already turn eight times a year may only add cover, while the same euro spent on an understocked boot size could recover lost sales.


### Finding the weak driver


A low return comes from a low margin, a slow turn, or both, and the remedy differs. For tents, the retailer can compare two moves on paper.


- Fewer end-of-season markdowns that raise the realised margin from 45% to 47% lift gross margin to €423k and the ratio to 1.28.
- Holding 10% less stock on average (€297k) for the same sales lifts it to 1.36.


Doing both gives 1.42. For this category the stock side has more to give than the margin side. Accessories are the reverse case: stock is already lean, and the 30% margin is the number to work on through pricing or purchasing terms.


### Going below the category


The same calculation works for a brand, a supplier, a product, or a store, as long as margin and average stock are measured on the same perimeter. Category averages usually conceal a wide spread. The buyers we work with often underestimate how much of a category's average inventory sits in variants that contribute very little margin, such as extreme sizes or last season's colours.


Ranking products by GMROI inside a category gives a short list for range reviews. A low rank does not mean a product should be delisted, since some products are there to complete an offer or to bring customers into the store. It does mean the product should be able to justify the stock it occupies.


## Where GMROI misleads


A ratio can improve while the business gets worse. Four limits are worth knowing before GMROI becomes anyone's target.


### It can rise while margin in euros falls


Amara manages the tents category (an illustrative case). Given a GMROI target, she cut average stock from €330k to €250k by reducing depth across the range. Bestsellers ran out during the peak weeks, and annual sales fell from €900k to €780k.


Gross margin dropped to €351k at the same 45% rate, so the ratio rose from 1.23 to 1.40. The target was met and the category earned €54k less. A return on inventory target needs a companion measure, such as gross margin in euros or availability on the top products.


### It ignores every cost below gross margin


Two categories with the same GMROI can cost very different amounts to run. Bulky tents take more floor area and more handling per euro of margin than gas canisters do. Retailers who want to capture this pair GMROI with gross margin per square metre of selling area (often called GMROF) or per labour hour (GMROL).


### It does not see lost sales


The numerator only contains margin on sales that happened. A product that is out of stock for three weeks shows a small average inventory and can post an excellent figure. Read the ratio next to an availability or lost sales measure, especially for products with long lead times.


### Short periods are distorted by timing


Monthly GMROI on seasonal goods swings with the calendar. Stock arrives weeks before the sales it supports, so pre-season months look poor and peak months look outstanding. A rolling 12 months, or the same weeks compared year on year, removes most of that noise, and a new product needs a full selling cycle before its figure means anything.


Most of these limits lead back to the denominator. Average inventory depends on how well each buy matched demand, product by product and store by store, and on how quickly replenishment corrects the gaps. That is the part[AI-driven inventory optimization](https://www.metreecs.com/inventory-optimization) works on: Metreecs forecasts demand per product and location every day and sizes stock to it, which lowers average inventory without the stockouts a blanket cut produces.


## FAQ


### What does a GMROI of 2 mean?


It means that over the period measured, each €1 of average inventory at cost generated €2 of gross margin. It does not mean the category made a profit, because rent, staff, logistics, and financing still come out of that margin. Whether 2 is good depends on the sector and on the category's own history.


### Is GMROI the same as inventory turnover?


No. Turnover (COGS divided by average inventory) measures how fast stock moves and ignores what each sale earns. GMROI adds the margin, since it equals turnover multiplied by gross margin over COGS. Two categories with the same turnover can have very different returns.


### Should I calculate GMROI at cost or at retail value?


Use inventory at cost. Gross margin is already net of cost, and dividing it by stock at retail value mixes two bases and understates the return. If your merchandising system only stores retail values, convert them with the category's cost ratio before dividing.


### How often should I review GMROI?


A rolling 12-month figure reviewed every month or every quarter suits most categories. Shorter windows are distorted by seasonality, because stock arrives before the sales it supports. The review that matters most is the one held before a buying cycle, when the result can still change a decision.


### Can I calculate GMROI for a single product or a single store?


Yes, as long as margin and average inventory cover exactly the same perimeter. At product level, use enough history to smooth out delivery timing. At store level, remember that warehouse stock held for that store is part of its investment too.


## Conclusion


GMROI puts margin and stock into one number, which makes it a fairer way to compare categories than margin rate or turnover alone. Calculate it with inventory at cost and a 13-point average, read it category by category, and pair it with margin in euros and availability so it cannot be gamed.
